title: The Writing Office & Message Centre
strapline: Real reasons to write — a list, a label, a letter to a friend.
intent: Children write for genuine purposes — lists, labels, notes, cards — so writing feels useful, not a chore.
Children discover that writing carries a message from one person to another, the whole point of print.
Children rehearse the tools and habits of a writer: choosing paper, gripping a pen, forming their letters.
Children practise writing their own name and the names of people who matter to them.
Children build the fine control, letter knowledge and left-to-right habit that formal writing needs.
implementation: Stock an office corner richly: varied paper, envelopes, pens, pencils, clipboards, stampers, a stapler, sticky notes, a message board.
Give writing a real audience — a message pigeonhole for each child, a notice board, a post box that's genuinely emptied.
Model writing for a purpose: 'I'll write a note to remind us', 'let's make a label so everyone knows'.
Value every attempt from scribble to letters — 'read me what you've written' — and respond to the meaning.
Keep name cards handy so children can copy or check their own name and their friends' names.
Link the office to the play across the room — signs for the block area, tickets for the train, a menu for the cafe.
Add a role — receptionist, postie, secretary — so writing has a job attached to it.
key_questions: What do you want to tell them?
Can you write your name on it so they know who it's from?
What could we write on the label?
Shall we post it — who will empty the box?

impact.text: Children write for a purpose — a list, label, note or card.
Children understand writing carries a message to a reader.
Children write their own name, or a good attempt at it.
Children form some recognisable letters with control.
Children choose tools and use them with a comfortable grip.
Children take on a writing role and sustain it in their play.

enhancements: A working post box emptied daily, with home-made stamps.
A pigeonhole or 'in-tray' for every child to receive notes.
Clipboards for writing on the move — taking orders, doing a survey.
Alphabet strips, name cards and a word bank of the children's interests.
A typewriter or old keyboard for another way to make print.
A greetings-card factory for birthdays and thank-yous.

playing_exploring: Children choose what to write and who to write to.
The tools and papers invite experimentation with print.
active_learning: Children persist to finish a card or letter that matters to them.
A real reader waiting gives writing a purpose worth the effort.
creating_thinking: Children plan a message and decide how to set it down.
They connect writing to their wider play, making signs and labels it needs.
